extracted.intended_audience: labor & employment attorneys; employers and HR professionals; unions and union representatives; policymakers and stakeholders in NLRB rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the NLRB (and courts) to determine when two or more entities are joint employers of particular employees under the National Labor Relations Act, including what counts as control and which employment terms are 'essential.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Control must bear on essential terms and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: A joint employer's control—whether direct or indirect, exercised or reserved—must bear on the essential terms and conditions of employment and not on the routine components of a company-to-company contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation (BFI v. NLRB): the control relevant to joint-employer status is control that affects essential employment terms; routine contractual arrangements between companies do not by themselves establish joint-employer status. Evaluate whether the alleged control actually pertains to essential terms and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential terms and conditions (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors drawn from the common law of agency relevant to the joint-employer inquiry include control over an employee's hiring, firing, training, promotion, discipline, and supervision; the final rule also uses phrasing such as 'tenure of employment, including hiring and discharge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list of essential terms and conditions is discussed further in the rule (Sec. V.D.). The Board treats matters relating to particular employees' hiring and discharge as essential, but clarifies that these examples are not intended to create per se rules for any industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect control (including through intermediaries) can be probative
rubrics_metrics.description: Control that is mediated or exercised through an intermediary is, by definition, indirect — but such indirect control can nevertheless be relevant and independently probative of joint-employer status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court guidance (BFI, D.C. Cir.): indirect control (e.g., authority exercised through intermediary employees or where supervisors merely ferry orders) may support a joint-employer finding on the specific factual record. Do not discount mediated/indirect acts simply because they are not immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserved or authorized rights to control are relevant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: An employer's authorized or reserved right to control (even if not actually exercised) is relevant evidence in the joint-employer inquiry under traditional common-law agency principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board and courts have held that an entity's reserved contractual authority to control matters can weigh toward joint-employer status. Lack of actual exercise does not automatically negate relevance of reserved authority; evaluate the scope and practical effect of reserved rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirement: common-law employment relationship with particular employees
rubrics_metrics.description: A putative joint employer must have a common-law employment relationship with the particular employees in question as a threshold requirement for a joint-employer finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where control is alleged, the Board will not treat entities as joint employers unless the essential elements of a common-law employment relationship with those particular employees are established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bargaining scope tied to authority to control essential terms
rubrics_metrics.description: If an entity is a putative joint employer, it must bargain over the essential terms and conditions of employment that it possesses the authority to control or over which it exercises the power to control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NPRM framing: the proposed rule would require bargaining only over those essential terms the putative joint employer has authority to control. When multiple statutory employers each possess some authority, it may serve the Act's purposes for them to be parties to bargaining over working conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total factual context and case-by-case adjudication using common-law agency principles
rubrics_metrics.description: What is important is that the total factual context be assessed in light of pertinent common-law agency principles; the Board's role is to flesh out the operation of the legal test through case-by-case adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not expect a single definitive formula; evaluate variant situations on their facts. The Board will apply an evolutionary, case-by-case approach rather than adopt categorical, bright-line rules for all contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: No per se or categorical treatment of industries or contracting relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board rejects treating particular industries or contracting arrangements (e.g., construction general contractors, hospitals, travel-nurse arrangements) as per se joint-employer situations; joint-employer status depends on all elements of the standard being met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments expressing concern about industry-specific effects are acknowledged, but the Board emphasizes that general contractors or hospitals will only be joint employers if the full standard—including the common-law employment relationship and control over essential terms—is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with traditional common-law agency sources (Restatement & cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board's standard looks to traditional common-law agency principles and precedent (including the Restatement (Second) of Agency and Supreme Court/circuit decisions) as relevant sources for the joint-employer analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should consider controlling precedents cited (e.g., Boire v. Greyhound; United Insurance Co.; Jewel Tea; Value Village; BFI) and the Restatement factors when assessing employer status; terminology (direct/indirect/reserved) reflects language from precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of health and safety and interplay with other regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Some commenters argued workplace health and safety historically was not regarded as an essential term under common law and should be omitted; the Board states it is aware that other federal agencies regulate substantive health and safety standards and does not intend to prescribe particular health and safety standards in the final rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When health and safety matters arise in the joint-employer analysis, take into account the existing regulatory roles of OSHA, FMCSA, and other agencies; the Board's rule does not attempt to set substantive health and safety standards, only to determine whether control over such matters bears on essential terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology reflects precedent but does not require taxonomy of control
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Board uses terms like 'direct,' 'indirect,' and 'reserved' control as reflected in precedent, the joint-employer analysis does not require that forms of control be categorized in any particular way; control is the touchstone regardless of how it is wielded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board intends the terminology to be descriptive of precedent, not to force a rigid taxonomy; evaluate whether control exists and whether it affects essential terms rather than relying solely on labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standard: evaluate whether entity possesses or exercises control over one or more essential terms for particular employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will consider all relevant evidence regarding whether a putative joint employer possesses or exercises the requisite control over one or more essential terms and conditions of particular employees' employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess concrete evidence (contracts, supervisory practices, actual exercises of authority, reserved rights, intermediary arrangements) bearing on control over essential employment terms for the particular employees at issue.
